chapter.name: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

questions.q: Changes in which only physical properties such as shape, size and state change, and no new substance is formed, are called:
questions.a: Physical changes. The chapter defines a physical change as one in which only physical properties like shape, size and state change and no new substance forms.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physical change?
o: Folding a sheet of paper into a fan
Burning a magnesium ribbon in air
Blowing exhaled air into lime water until it turns milky
questions.a: Folding a sheet of paper into a fan. Only the shape of the paper changes and it is still paper; the other three form new substances.

questions.q: Define a physical change and give one example of a physical change that happens in the kitchen.
s: Definition: a change in which only physical properties such as shape, size or state change and no new substance is formed
A kitchen example, such as chopping vegetables, boiling water or melting ice cubes
questions.a: A physical change is a change in which only physical properties such as shape, size or state change and no new substance is formed. Example: chopping vegetables (or boiling water, or melting ice).

questions.q: True or False: When a balloon is inflated and the air is then let out, the rubber of the balloon is still the same material. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: only the size and shape of the balloon changed; no new substance was formed, so it is a physical change
questions.a: True. Inflating and deflating the balloon changes only its size and shape; the rubber sheet remains rubber and no new substance is formed.

questions.q: Match each change in Column I with its correct description in Column II. Column I: 1. Folding paper into a boat  2. Burning a magnesium ribbon  3. Blowing exhaled air into lime water  4. Melting ice cubes. Column II: (p) physical change in which the state changes  (q) physical change in which only the shape changes  (r) chemical change that gives out heat and light  (s) chemical change that forms an insoluble white substance.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-r, 3-s, 4-p: folding changes only shape; burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide with heat and light; lime water forms insoluble white calcium carbonate; melting ice changes state from solid to liquid.

questions.q: Gita folds a sheet of paper into a boat and later unfolds it. The flat sheet now has creases. Mohan says, 'The creases show that a new substance has formed.' Which reply is best?
o: The creases are only a change in appearance; the material is still paper, so the change is physical.
Mohan is right, because the sheet does not look exactly as it did before.
Mohan is right, because any change that leaves a mark is a chemical change.
The change is physical only because no heat was used, so the creases do not matter.
questions.a: The creases are only a change in appearance; the material is still paper, so the change is physical. A change in appearance alone does not mean a new substance formed.

questions.q: Arjun says: 'In every physical change, the state of the substance changes.' Check his claim using three changes from the chapter: folding paper, crushing chalk into powder and melting ice. Is he right?
s: Folding paper: the paper stays a solid; only its shape changes, yet it is a physical change
Crushing chalk: the chalk stays a solid; only its size changes, yet it is a physical change; only melting ice changes state (solid to liquid)
So the claim is wrong: in a physical change the state may or may not change; what matters is that no new substance forms
questions.a: Arjun is wrong. Folding paper and crushing chalk are physical changes in which the material stays solid and only shape or size changes; only melting ice changes state. In a physical change the state may or may not change; the test is that no new substance is formed.

questions.q: Making chapatis at home: (i) dough is made into small balls, (ii) the balls are rolled into flat chapatis, (iii) each chapati is cooked on a hot tawa, and (iv) the tawa is heated by burning cooking gas in the stove. (a) Classify each of the four steps as a physical or a chemical change, with a reason for each. (b) Riya says, 'A cooked chapati is still flat and round like the rolled dough, so the whole process is physical.' Judge her claim.
s: (i) Making balls: physical; only the shape of the dough changes and no new substance forms
(ii) Rolling into chapatis: physical; only shape and size change
(iii) Cooking on the tawa: chemical; cooking is a chemical change that forms new substances and the raw dough cannot be got back
(iv) Burning gas: chemical; it is combustion, a reaction with oxygen giving heat and light
(b) Riya is wrong: keeping the same shape does not decide the kind of change; cooking forms new substances, so the process has both physical and chemical changes
questions.a: (i) and (ii) are physical changes: only the shape and size of the dough change and it is still dough. (iii) Cooking is a chemical change (the chapter lists cooking with combustion and rusting); new substances form and the raw dough cannot be got back. (iv) Burning gas is combustion, a chemical change giving heat and light. (b) Riya is wrong: shape is not the test. Cooking forms new substances, so making chapatis involves both physical and chemical changes.

questions.q: The turning of lime water milky is used as a test for which gas?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide. The chapter says the turning of lime water milky is used as a test for carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Two tumblers hold equal amounts of fresh lime water. Exhaled air is blown into tumbler P through a straw for one minute; tumbler Q is left untouched beside it. After an hour, a white layer has settled at the bottom of P only. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: A new insoluble substance formed in P from the carbon dioxide in exhaled air, so a chemical change took place.
Dust from the room settled in P, because P was disturbed by the straw.
The bubbles of exhaled air sank to the bottom of P and became the white layer.
Some lime water in P evaporated and left the white layer behind, which is a physical change.
questions.a: A new insoluble substance (calcium carbonate) formed in P from the carbon dioxide in exhaled air, so a chemical change took place. Q, kept under the same conditions without exhaled air, shows no layer, so dust or evaporation cannot explain it.

questions.q: True or False: Mixing vinegar with baking soda is a physical change, because only bubbles appear. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a new substance, carbon dioxide, is formed (it turns lime water milky), so it is a chemical change
questions.a: False. Mixing vinegar with baking soda forms a new substance, carbon dioxide gas, which turns lime water milky. Since a new substance forms, it is a chemical change.

questions.q: (a) Write the word equation for the reaction that takes place when carbon dioxide is passed into lime water. (b) Which product makes the lime water look milky?
s: (a) Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide gives Calcium carbonate + Water
(b) Calcium carbonate, a white substance that is insoluble in water
questions.a: (a) Calcium hydroxide (lime water) + Carbon dioxide gives Calcium carbonate + Water. (b) Calcium carbonate: it is white and insoluble in water, so the liquid looks milky.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Lime water turns milky when exhaled air is blown into it. Reason (R): The calcium carbonate formed in the reaction is insoluble in water.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form white calcium carbonate, which does not dissolve in water, so the liquid looks milky.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: Blowing exhaled air into tap water produces bubbles only, with no change in the appearance of the water. Statement II: A small amount of water is also formed when carbon dioxide reacts with lime water. Statement III: The fizzing of vinegar with baking soda is a physical change, because no new substance is formed. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong: vinegar and baking soda form a new substance, carbon dioxide, so the change is a chemical change.

questions.q: Riya puts two teaspoons of lemon juice in a small bottle, adds a pinch of baking soda and quickly stretches a balloon over the mouth of the bottle. The mixture fizzes and the balloon swells. (a) Name the gas that fills the balloon. (b) How can she show that it is this gas? (c) Is the change in the bottle physical or chemical? Give a reason.
s: (a) Carbon dioxide
(b) Pass the gas from the balloon into freshly prepared lime water; it turns milky
(c) Chemical, because a new substance (carbon dioxide) is formed
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide. (b) Let the gas from the balloon pass into freshly prepared lime water; the lime water turns milky. (c) It is a chemical change, because a new substance, carbon dioxide, is formed.

questions.q: At a kitchen science fair in Bhopal, Imran puts a teaspoon of vinegar in a small used bottle and adds a pinch of baking soda. He has fixed a flexible straw from this bottle into a second bottle holding freshly prepared lime water. Visitors hear a fizzing, bubbling sound and see gas bubbles in the first bottle. A few seconds later the lime water in the second bottle turns milky. (a) What sound do the visitors hear in the first bottle? (b) Why does the lime water turn milky? (c) Name the gas that travels through the straw. (d) Is the change in the first bottle physical or chemical?
s: (a) A fizzing, bubbling sound
(b) Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water and forms calcium carbonate, a white substance that is insoluble in water
(c) Carbon dioxide
(d) Chemical, because a new substance, carbon dioxide, is formed
questions.a: (a) A fizzing, bubbling sound. (b) Carbon dioxide reacts with the lime water and forms calcium carbonate, a white substance that does not dissolve in water, so the liquid looks milky. (c) Carbon dioxide. (d) A chemical change, because a new substance (carbon dioxide) is formed: vinegar + baking soda gives carbon dioxide + other substances.

questions.q: Reema takes three test tubes. To each she adds a pinch of baking soda. Then she adds a teaspoon of plain water to tube 1, lemon juice to tube 2 and vinegar to tube 3. (a) In which tubes will she see bubbles of gas? (b) How should she test the gas, and what result does she expect? (c) Classify the change in the tubes that give gas as physical or chemical, with a reason. (d) Write the word equation for the change in tube 3. (e) Her friend says, 'Tube 1 also had baking soda, so it must give the same gas.' Explain why tube 1 does not support this.
s: (a) Tubes 2 and 3 (lemon juice and vinegar)
(b) Pass the gas into freshly prepared lime water; it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide
(c) Chemical, because a new substance (carbon dioxide) is formed
(d) Vinegar + Baking soda gives Carbon dioxide + Other substances
(e) Tube 1 gives no bubbles, so no carbon dioxide forms; baking soda alone is not enough, the vinegar or lemon juice is needed for the reaction
questions.a: (a) Tubes 2 and 3. (b) Pass the gas into freshly prepared lime water; it turns milky, so the gas is carbon dioxide. (c) Chemical changes, because a new substance, carbon dioxide, is formed. (d) Vinegar + Baking soda gives Carbon dioxide + Other substances. (e) Baking soda with plain water gives no bubbles, so no carbon dioxide forms; the gas comes from the reaction of baking soda with vinegar or lemon juice, not from baking soda alone.

questions.q: A chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat and/or light is called:
questions.a: Combustion. The chapter defines combustion as a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat and/or light.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a combustible substance?
questions.a: A stone. The chapter gives wood, paper, cotton and kerosene as examples of combustible substances; a stone does not burn.

questions.q: Fireflies give out light by a chemical change, without producing heat. What is this kind of light production in living organisms called?
questions.a: Bioluminescence: light produced without heat in living organisms, as in fireflies.

questions.q: A few iron nails left on a damp tray for a week are covered with a brown coating. (a) Name the brown substance and give its chemical name. (b) Why is this a chemical change?
s: (a) Rust; iron oxide
(b) A new substance (iron oxide) is formed
questions.a: (a) Rust, which is iron oxide. (b) It is a chemical change because a new brown-coloured substance, iron oxide, is formed.

questions.q: Your class is making a fire-safety poster for the school corridor. Answer each part in one line for the poster. (a) What is combustion? (b) Name two combustible substances found in a classroom. (c) Which component of air supports combustion? (d) What should be done at once if a person's clothes catch fire? (e) What kind of blanket should never be used for this, and why?
s: (a) A chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and gives heat and/or light
(b) Any two, such as paper, wood or cotton
(c) Oxygen
(d) Wrap a blanket or cloth around the person to cut off the supply of air
(e) A synthetic blanket or cloth, because it can melt and stick to the skin
questions.a: (a) Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and gives heat and/or light. (b) Paper and wood (or cotton). (c) Oxygen. (d) Wrap a blanket or cloth around the person; this cuts off the air supply and the fire goes out. (e) Never a synthetic blanket or cloth, because it can melt and stick to the skin.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A burning candle covered with a glass tumbler stops burning after some time. Reason (R): Carbon dioxide is the component of air that supports combustion.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The covered candle goes out because it has no continuous supply of air; the component of air that supports combustion is oxygen, not carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Rusting of iron and burning of a magnesium ribbon are both chemical changes, so both must give out light.' Check his claim.
s: Both are chemical changes: rusting forms iron oxide and burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide
Burning magnesium is combustion and gives heat and light, but rusting is described only as forming a new brown substance, with no light
So the claim is wrong: a chemical change is known by the new substance formed, not by light; giving light is a feature of combustion
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Both are chemical changes because new substances form (iron oxide and magnesium oxide). But only burning magnesium is combustion with heat and light; rusting just forms a brown substance. A chemical change is recognised by the new substance, not by light.

questions.q: In a Class 7 demonstration in Kochi, the teacher holds a short magnesium ribbon with tongs over a watch glass and lights it. It burns with a dazzling white light, the students feel heat, and a white powder collects in the watch glass. On the same day she places a few iron nails on wet cotton in a dish. A week later the nails have a brown coating that cannot be wiped back into shiny iron. (a) Name the white powder. (b) Write the word equation for the burning of the ribbon. (c) Name the brown substance on the nails. (d) Which of the two changes is combustion? Give a reason.
s: (a) Magnesium oxide
(b) Magnesium + Oxygen gives Magnesium oxide + Heat + Light
(c) Rust (iron oxide)
(d) Burning of the magnesium ribbon, because it reacts with oxygen and produces heat and light
questions.a: (a) Magnesium oxide. (b) Magnesium + Oxygen gives Magnesium oxide + Heat + Light. (c) Rust, that is iron oxide. (d) The burning of magnesium is combustion: it reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light. Rusting forms a new substance too, but gives no heat or light that the students could see.

questions.q: A candle burned inside a tall jar with its lid on until the flame went out. The lid is lifted for just a moment and a second lit candle is quickly lowered into the jar. What is most likely to happen?
o: The second candle soon goes out, because too little oxygen is left in the jar and it now holds carbon dioxide.
The second candle burns longer than in open air, because the jar is already warm.
The second candle burns normally for as long as in open air, because the jar still contains air.
The second candle burns brighter, because carbon dioxide in the jar supports combustion.
questions.a: The second candle soon goes out. The covered first candle went out because it had no continuous supply of air; too little oxygen, the part of air that supports combustion, is left, and the jar now holds carbon dioxide formed by the burning, so it cannot keep a flame going.

questions.q: The minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire is called its:
questions.a: Ignition temperature: the minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire.

questions.q: In the fire triangle, what does the word 'fuel' stand for?
o: The smoke given out by a fire
questions.a: A combustible substance. The fire triangle lists a combustible substance (fuel), oxygen, and heat that lets the fuel reach its ignition temperature.

questions.q: Name the three requirements for combustion shown in the fire triangle.
s: A combustible substance (fuel) and oxygen
Heat that allows the fuel to reach its ignition temperature
questions.a: The three requirements are: a combustible substance (fuel), oxygen, and heat that allows the fuel to reach its ignition temperature.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: The three requirements for combustion are a fuel, oxygen, and heat that lets the fuel reach its ignition temperature. Statement II: The ignition temperature of a substance is the highest temperature it reaches while it is burning. Statement III: A substance can start burning even when no flame touches it. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: the ignition temperature is the minimum (lowest) temperature at which a substance catches fire, not the highest temperature it reaches. Paper heated by focused sunrays catches fire without any flame, which supports Statement III.

questions.q: Three actions are taken during a small fire: (i) a cotton blanket is wrapped round a person whose clothes have caught fire; (ii) the unburnt sheets of paper lying next to a burning sheet are carried away; (iii) a burning candle is covered with a glass tumbler. Which requirement of the fire triangle does each action take away?
questions.a: (i) oxygen, (ii) fuel, (iii) oxygen. The blanket and the tumbler both cut off the supply of air, so oxygen is taken away; carrying away the unburnt paper removes the combustible substance (fuel) the fire could spread to.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Pouring sand over a small fire of dry leaves puts the fire out. Reason (R): Combustion needs a fuel, oxygen and heat together, and the sand cuts off the supply of oxygen to the leaves.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: all three sides of the fire triangle are needed, and covering the leaves with sand stops oxygen from reaching them, so the fire goes out.

questions.q: Divya notices that a newspaper has been lying on her table for a month without catching fire. She says, 'This shows paper is not a combustible substance.' Check her claim using the fire triangle.
s: Paper is a combustible substance (fuel); the chapter lists it with wood, cotton and kerosene
The newspaper has fuel and oxygen from the air, but nothing heats it to its ignition temperature
So the claim is wrong: the paper did not burn because one requirement, heat, was missing, not because it cannot burn
questions.a: Divya is wrong. Paper is a combustible substance. Lying on the table it has fuel and oxygen, but nothing heats it up to its ignition temperature. One side of the fire triangle (heat) is missing, so it does not burn; it still can burn when that heat is given.

questions.q: For its Deepavali assembly, the school will light rows of diyas on the stage, close to cloth curtains and paper decorations. Write four fire-safety rules for the event. Link each rule to one requirement of the fire triangle (fuel, oxygen or heat) or to a caution given in the chapter, and say in each case how the rule prevents or stops a fire.
s: Rule 1: a valid fire-safety rule correctly linked to a fire-triangle requirement or a chapter caution, saying how it prevents or stops a fire
Rule 2: a second valid rule, correctly linked and explained in the same way
Rule 3: a third valid rule, correctly linked and explained in the same way
Rule 4: a fourth valid rule, correctly linked and explained in the same way
questions.a: Any four valid rules, each correctly linked, earn the marks. Sample rules: (1) Keep the diyas well away from curtains and paper decorations, so this fuel is not heated to its ignition temperature (fuel and heat). (2) Do not leave a lens or glass object where it can focus sunrays on the paper decorations; focused sunrays can heat paper to its ignition temperature without any flame (heat). (3) Keep a cotton blanket ready; if anyone's clothes catch fire, wrap it round the person to cut off the supply of air (oxygen). (4) Never use a synthetic blanket or cloth for this, as it can melt and stick to the skin (chapter caution).

questions.q: Sana and Tom repeat Activity 5.6 at 1 pm on a sunny day, under their teacher's supervision, using identical sheets of paper. Trial 1: a sheet held with tongs is touched by a lighted matchstick; it catches fire in about 1 second. Trial 2: sunrays are focused by a magnifying glass to the smallest, brightest spot on a sheet; smoke appears at 50 seconds and the sheet catches fire at 70 seconds. Trial 3: a sheet is left on the desk in the shade for one hour; it does not catch fire. (a) Which two requirements for combustion are present in all three trials? (b) Why does the sheet in Trial 3 not burn? (c) Why does Trial 1 take much less time than Trial 2? (d) Tom concludes, 'A fire is always needed to start burning.' Judge his conclusion using the data.
s: (a) Fuel (the paper) and oxygen (the air)
(b) Nothing heats it to its ignition temperature, so the third requirement, heat, is missing
(c) The matchstick flame is already hotter than the ignition temperature of paper, while the focused sunrays take time to raise the paper to it
(d) Wrong: in Trial 2 the paper caught fire with no flame at all; what is needed is heat to reach the ignition temperature, not a fire
questions.a: (a) The paper (fuel) and oxygen from the air. (b) Nothing raises its temperature to the ignition temperature, so the heat requirement is missing. (c) The matchstick is already hotter than the ignition temperature of paper, so it catches almost at once; the focused sunrays have to heat the paper gradually, so it takes 70 seconds. (d) Tom is wrong: Trial 2 shows paper catching fire without any flame. Burning needs heat enough to reach the ignition temperature, not necessarily a fire.

questions.q: When a candle burns, which of the following is a chemical change?
o: Solidifying of wax drips at the base
questions.a: Burning of the wax vapour. Melting, solidifying and evaporation of wax are physical changes; the burning of the vapour is a chemical change.

questions.q: Match each event at a burning candle in Column I with the correct description in Column II. Column I: 1. Solid wax near the flame turns liquid  2. Liquid wax moves up to the flame  3. Liquid wax turns into vapour  4. Wax vapour burns to give a flame. Column II: (p) evaporation, a physical change  (q) melting, a physical change  (r) a chemical change  (s) carried up the wick.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-p, 4-r: wax melts (physical), is carried up the wick, evaporates (physical), and its vapour burns to give the flame (chemical).

questions.q: Assertion (A): The burning of a candle involves both physical and chemical changes. Reason (R): The melting of wax is a physical change, while the burning of wax vapour is a chemical change.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: melting (and evaporation) of wax are physical changes, and burning of the vapour is a chemical change, so both kinds occur in one process.

questions.q: True or False: Carbon dioxide is one of the substances formed when a candle burns. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: carbon from the wax combines with oxygen from the air to form carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky
questions.a: True. When the candle burns, carbon from the wax and oxygen from the air form carbon dioxide; lime water placed under a tumbler covering the candle turns milky.

questions.q: Answer these about a lit candle. (a) What happens to the wax near the flame? (b) How does the liquid wax reach the flame? (c) What actually burns to produce the flame?
s: (a) It melts (and then evaporates due to the heat of the flame)
(b) It is carried up the wick
(c) The vapour of the wax
questions.a: (a) The wax melts due to the heat of the flame. (b) The liquid wax is carried up the wick. (c) The wax vapour burns to produce the flame.

questions.q: Ravi collects the hardened wax drips from a candle, melts them and makes them solid again. He says, 'So the whole burning of a candle can be reversed.' (a) Which part of the candle's changes can be reversed? (b) Which part cannot, and why?
s: (a) The melting and solidifying of wax (physical changes) can be reversed
(b) The burning of the wax vapour cannot, because it is a chemical change that forms new substances such as carbon dioxide
questions.a: (a) Melting and solidifying of wax are physical changes, so that part can be reversed. (b) The burning of wax vapour is a chemical change that forms new substances such as carbon dioxide, so the burnt wax cannot be got back. Ravi is only partly right.

questions.q: An ice cube left in the sun and a lit candle both become smaller on the same table. Compare the two in three respects: (a) the kind of change, (b) whether a new substance forms, (c) whether the lost material can be got back.
s: (a) Ice: only a physical change (melting); candle: both physical changes (melting, evaporation) and a chemical change (burning of vapour)
(b) Ice: no new substance, it is still water; candle: new substances such as carbon dioxide form when the vapour burns
(c) The melted water can be refrozen into ice, but the wax that has burnt cannot be got back as wax
questions.a: (a) The ice cube only melts, a physical change; the candle melts and evaporates (physical) and its vapour burns (chemical). (b) Melted ice is still water, with no new substance; burning wax vapour forms new substances such as carbon dioxide. (c) The water can be refrozen into ice, but the burnt wax cannot be got back.

questions.q: Michael Faraday believed that a candle was the perfect object to introduce scientific study. Support or reject his view using what a single candle shows. (a) Name two physical changes seen in a burning candle. (b) Name the chemical change. (c) Describe how you could show that a new substance forms when a candle burns. (d) What happens if the burning candle is covered with a glass tumbler, and what does this show? (e) A student says, 'A candle is a poor object for teaching because it shows only one kind of change.' Judge this statement.
s: (a) Any two of: melting of wax, evaporation of wax, solidification of wax drips
(b) The burning of wax vapour
(c) Cover the burning candle with a glass tumbler and add a little lime water; it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide has formed
(d) The flame goes out after some time because the air supply is cut off; this shows oxygen is needed for combustion
(e) The student is wrong: one candle shows both physical and chemical changes and the need for oxygen, so Faraday's view is supported
questions.a: (a) Melting of wax and its evaporation (also solidifying of drips). (b) Burning of the wax vapour. (c) Cover the candle with a glass tumbler and add a small amount of lime water to the petri dish; it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide (a new substance) has formed. (d) The flame goes out after some time since it has no continuous supply of air; oxygen is needed for combustion. (e) The student is wrong: a single candle shows physical changes, a chemical change and the role of oxygen, which supports Faraday's view.

questions.q: Which of the following changes can be reversed?
o: Condensing water vapour back into liquid water
questions.a: Condensing water vapour back into liquid water. Water that evaporates can be condensed back, and the liquid can be evaporated again; chopped vegetables, popcorn and burnt wood cannot return to their original form.

questions.q: Which of the following is a desirable change?
o: Release of substances from drying paint
questions.a: Milk changing into curd. The chapter lists it among useful (desirable) changes; rusting and decay of stored food are undesirable, and drying paint causes atmospheric pollution.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: Ripening of fruits is a desirable change. Statement II: Rusting of iron is an undesirable change. Statement III: Every change that cannot be reversed is an undesirable change. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong: cutting fruits cannot be undone (like chopped vegetables), yet the chapter calls it a desirable change, as it does cooking of food.

questions.q: True or False: A change that is undesirable in one situation can be desirable in another situation. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: decomposition of food is undesirable during storage, but it is useful when food waste is turned into compost
questions.a: True. Decay of food during storage is undesirable, but the decomposition of food waste is very useful for making compost.

questions.q: Town P had 2,000 cars ten years ago and has 4,000 cars today. Town Q had 5,000 cars ten years ago and still has 5,000. Every car burns the same amount of fuel in a year. (a) In which town has the carbon dioxide added to the air by cars each year gone up over the ten years? (b) In which town do the cars add more carbon dioxide each year today? Give a reason for each.
s: (a) Town P: its cars doubled, so more fuel is burnt and more carbon dioxide is added each year; Town Q is unchanged
(b) Town Q: it has 5,000 cars against 4,000 in P, so more fuel is burnt there and more carbon dioxide is added
questions.a: (a) Town P, because its cars have doubled from 2,000 to 4,000, so more fuel is burnt each year and the carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere has gone up; in Q the number has not changed. (b) Town Q, because today it has 5,000 cars against P's 4,000, so it burns more fuel and adds more carbon dioxide each year.

questions.q: A dairy turns milk into curd to sell. At the tea stall next door, a can of milk kept overnight for the morning tea has turned into curd. Which statement best describes the two events?
o: The same change is desirable for the dairy and undesirable for the tea stall, so whether a change is desirable depends on the situation.
The change is desirable in both places, because the chapter lists milk turning into curd as a desirable change.
The change is undesirable in both places, because curd cannot be turned back into milk.
The change is desirable at the dairy only because there it is a chemical change, while at the tea stall it is a physical change.
questions.a: The same change is desirable for the dairy and undesirable for the tea stall. Milk turning into curd is a useful change for the dairy, but the tea stall needed milk; a change that is undesirable in some situations may be desirable in others. It is the same kind of change in both places.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Making popcorn from corn is a change that cannot be reversed. Reason (R): Cooking of food is a desirable change.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true but R does not explain A. Popcorn cannot go back to corn because the original form cannot be got back; whether a change is desirable has nothing to do with whether it can be reversed.

questions.q: Sohan says: 'Any change that cannot be reversed must be a chemical change.' Check his claim using chopping vegetables as an example.
s: Chopped vegetables cannot return to their original size and shape, so the change cannot be reversed
But chopping forms no new substance; only size and shape change, so it is a physical change
So the claim is wrong: whether a change can be reversed does not decide whether it is physical or chemical
questions.a: Sohan is wrong. Chopped vegetables cannot be returned to their original size and shape, so the change cannot be reversed; yet no new substance forms, only size and shape change, so it is a physical change. Being irreversible does not make a change chemical.

questions.q: A school must take 40 students and teachers to a science centre and back. Plan A: 10 cars, each using 4 litres of fuel for the round trip. Plan B: one bus using 15 litres for the round trip. Plan C: 2 vans, each using 9 litres for the round trip. A teacher says, 'Plan C is the best for the environment because vans are smaller than a bus.' (a) Find the total fuel each plan uses. (b) State how burning this fuel affects the atmosphere over the years. (c) Which plan should the school choose? (d) Judge the teacher's claim.
s: (a) Plan A 40 litres, Plan B 15 litres, Plan C 18 litres
(b) Burning fuel in vehicles increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, a long-term environmental impact
(c) Plan B, the bus, as it burns the least fuel (15 litres; 25 litres less than Plan A)
(d) The claim is wrong: the two vans together burn 18 litres, 3 litres more than the bus, so the size of a single vehicle does not decide it; the total fuel burnt does
questions.a: (a) Plan A: 10 x 4 = 40 litres; Plan B: 15 litres; Plan C: 2 x 9 = 18 litres. (b) The increased consumption of fuel by vehicles increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. (c) Plan B, the bus, burns the least fuel, so it adds the least carbon dioxide. (d) The teacher is wrong: the two vans together burn 18 litres, 3 litres more than the bus; what matters is the total fuel burnt, not the size of each vehicle.

questions.q: What are the heaps of sand, soil and stones lying at the base of mountains called?
questions.a: Sediments. The chapter calls the heaps of sand, soil and stones at the base of mountains sediments.

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II. Column I: 1. Weathering  2. Erosion  3. Sediments  4. Basalt. Column II: (p) a black-coloured rock that contains iron  (q) breaking down and moving of rock pebbles, soil and sediments by wind and flowing water  (r) physical and chemical changes in rocks that eventually lead to the formation of soil  (s) sand, soil and stones lying at the base of mountains.
questions.a: 1-r, 2-q, 3-s, 4-p: weathering is the physical and chemical changes in rocks that form soil; erosion moves broken material by wind and water; sediments are the heaps at the base of mountains; basalt is a black iron-containing rock.

questions.q: Name any two natural causes that break large rocks into smaller pieces by physical changes.
s: First cause, any one of: temperature changes due to climatic conditions, growing roots of trees, freezing of water within cracks
Second cause, a different one from the same list
questions.a: Any two of: temperature changes due to climatic conditions; growing roots of trees; freezing of water within cracks in the rocks.

questions.q: True or False: The changes caused by erosion can easily be reversed within a few years. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False
Correct statement: most of these changes take place over thousands of years and cannot be reversed
questions.a: False. Most changes due to erosion, and the hardening of sediments into new rocks, take place over thousands of years and cannot be reversed.

questions.q: On a school trip to a hilly area, Class 7 students made notes. At the foot of a cliff lay a heap of sand, soil and stones. The roots of a large tree had grown into a crack in a big rock and split it. Near a waterfall, a black rock containing iron had a red layer on its surface. The pebbles in the stream were smooth, and fine sand had settled where the stream entered a calm lake. (a) Name one cause of physical weathering seen on the trip. (b) Name the red substance on the black rock. (c) Which process made the stream pebbles smooth? (d) Why did the fine sand settle in the lake?
s: (a) Growing roots of the tree splitting the rock
(b) Iron oxide
(c) Erosion by the flowing water
(d) The speed of the water decreased in the lake, so the carried material settled at the bottom
questions.a: (a) The growing roots of the tree that split the rock. (b) Iron oxide, formed when the iron-containing rock was exposed for a long time to water or moist air. (c) Erosion by the constantly flowing water. (d) In the lake the water slows down, so the material it carried settles at the bottom.

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'Weathering and erosion are just two names for the same thing.' Write a four-point answer that corrects him, comparing what happens to the rock, the kinds of change involved, the causes and the final result of each.
s: What happens: weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces or changes their composition; erosion breaks down and moves pebbles, soil and sediments from one place to another
Kinds of change: weathering includes both physical changes and chemical changes (water or chemicals in water reacting with the rock); erosion, as during a landslide, is a physical change
Causes: weathering by temperature changes, roots, freezing water and water or air with water vapour; erosion by wind and flowing water
Result: weathering eventually forms soil; eroded material settles where water or wind slows and hardens into new rocks
questions.a: They are different. (1) Weathering breaks rocks or changes their composition; erosion breaks down and also carries material to another place. (2) Weathering includes physical and chemical changes (water or chemicals in water reacting with the rock); erosion is a physical change. (3) Weathering is caused by temperature changes, roots, freezing water and moisture; erosion by wind and flowing water. (4) Weathering leads to soil; eroded sediments settle and harden into new rocks.

questions.q: For many years a boulder of basalt on a hillside is acted on by three things: tree roots growing into its cracks, water freezing inside its cracks, and moist air on its surface. Classify the change caused by each as physical or chemical, giving the evidence or product, and state what these changes together eventually lead to.
s: Roots and freezing water: physical changes; they break the rock into smaller pieces without forming a new substance
Moist air: a chemical change; the iron in basalt forms a red layer of iron oxide, a new substance
Together these are weathering, which eventually leads to the formation of soil
questions.a: Tree roots and freezing water break the rock into smaller pieces: physical changes with no new substance. Moist air reacts with the iron in basalt and forms a red layer of iron oxide: a chemical change. Together these physical and chemical changes are weathering, which eventually forms soil.

questions.q: Five events in the long life of a piece of rock are given out of order. P: fine sand collects on the floor of a lake. Q: a large rock high on a hillside splits into smaller pieces as water freezes in its cracks. R: over a very long time the layers of sand on the lake floor harden. S: a fast stream carries the pieces downhill, and they break into smaller, smoother bits. T: the stream enters the lake and its water slows down. (a) Arrange the events in the correct order. (b) Name the process in Q and the process in S. (c) Why does the sand collect at P and not in the fast stream? (d) What does event R finally produce? (e) Is the change in S physical or chemical? Give a reason.
s: (a) Q, S, T, P, R
(b) Q is weathering (a physical change caused by water freezing in cracks); S is erosion by flowing water
(c) When the speed of the water decreases, as in a lake, the material it carries settles at the bottom
(d) New rocks
(e) Physical: the pieces only become smaller and smoother and no new substance is formed; erosion by flowing water is a physical change
questions.a: (a) Q, S, T, P, R. (b) Q is weathering: freezing of water within cracks breaks the rock (a physical change). S is erosion: flowing water moves the pieces and makes them smaller and smoother. (c) In the lake the speed of the water decreases, so the material it was carrying settles at the bottom. (d) The sediments harden over time and become new rocks. (e) A physical change: the pieces change only in size and shape, no new substance forms; the chapter says erosion caused by flowing water is a physical change.
